pages.title: Can Meta’s Fiber Partner Corning Capitalize On Rising AI Fiber Prices? - AOL
pages.text:
Prices for specialized optical fiber used inside AI data centers are forecast to average more than five times their 2025 levels this year.
That could be good news for Corning Incorporated (NYSE:GLW), a major manufacturer of fiber-optic cables and connectivity equipment. The company has a supply agreement worth up to $6 billion with Meta Platforms Inc. (NASDAQ:META).
Corning’s Optical Communications business is already booming. Second-quarter sales jumped 32% to $2.07 billion, while segment net income surged 77% to $438 million.
But CEO Wendell Weeks says higher fiber prices aren’t the main reason.
Why Higher Fiber Prices Aren’t the Whole Story
TrendForce released new research Monday forecasting a global optical fiber shortage of 180 million fiber-kilometers this year, with shortages potentially lasting until 2028.TrendForce puts industry capacity utilization at 92%, while inventories have fallen to just one month’s supply. Expanding production typically takes 18 to 24 months.
As fiber supplies tighten, major customers are signing long-term agreements to secure future deliveries.
Corning’s agreement with Meta runs through 2030 and covers fiber, cables and connectivity products. Meta will also serve as the main customer for an expansion of Corning’s North Carolina cable factory, giving the manufacturer committed demand as it increases production.
During July’s earnings call, Wolfe Research analyst George Notter questioned Weeks about rising prices and the company’s growing reliance on long-term agreements.
“The price is higher, but that really isn’t how we’re driving that profitability improvement,” Weeks said.
Instead, Weeks credited higher-value connectivity products that help customers build networks faster and more cheaply.
Weeks added that Corning could sell more of its newest products if it had the capacity to manufacture them.
Wall Street Remains Bullish Despite Selloff
Corning shares have lost roughly half their value since hitting a record high in June, despite booming demand for its optical products.
UBS raised its price target for Corning to $201 earlier this month, maintaining a Buy rating. Citi is even more bullish, with a $220 target, while Bernstein is more cautious at $140.
On Polymarket, traders put roughly 28% odds on Corning’s third-quarter optical revenue exceeding $2.3 billion, although trading volume is just $3,500.
Meanwhile, a separate Polymarket puts roughly 9% odds on an AI industry downturn meeting the contract’s specific conditions by year-end, with more than $3 million traded on the market.
Meta reports earnings Wednesday, Oct. 21, followed by Corning on Oct. 27.

3M Jumps 6% on Expanded Amazon Data Center Deal and Earnings Beat; Coherent Edges Higher, Corning Stays Flat
3M surged past its industrial peers and the broader market on the same day it revealed a complex new Amazon arrangement that ties potential billions in revenue to conditions that have not yet been met.
Published October 20, 2026, 10:58am ET · 3 min read
3M (NYSE:MMM | MMM Price Prediction) stock jumped 6% to $171.91 as investors weighed an expanded Amazon (NASDAQ:AMZN) data center relationship alongside better-than-expected quarterly earnings. The company also raised its full-year adjusted earnings outlook, giving investors both a near-term profitability catalyst and a longer-term infrastructure opportunity.
The advance outpaced Coherent (NYSE:COHR) stock, which gained 1.33% to $235.11, while Corning (NYSE:GLW) stock was essentially flat, slipping 0.21% to $132.46. Those moves put 3M stock well ahead of the two peers today.
Amazon Agreement Expands the Opportunity
3M expanded its commercial relationship with Amazon to deploy and scale optical connectivity and other data center products. The agreement gives 3M a potential growth opportunity as Amazon invests in infrastructure supporting cloud computing and AI workloads.
As part of the arrangement, 3M issued an Amazon subsidiary a seven-year warrant to purchase up to approximately 3.16 million 3M shares at $164.89 each. About 85% of the warrant shares vest based on Amazon’s purchases of data center products, with that portion fully vesting once cumulative payments reach $6 billion.
The remaining 15% depends on separate milestone conditions, making the arrangement more nuanced than an immediate $6 billion order. For 3M, the commercial upside depends on purchases materializing over time, while an eventual warrant exercise could increase the company’s share count.
3M reported third-quarter adjusted earnings of $2.50 per share, exceeding the $2.39 consensus estimate cited in one earnings analysis. Revenue of approximately $6.6 billion was broadly in line with expectations, making profitability the clearer quarterly surprise.
The company reported adjusted organic sales growth of 3.3%, while GAAP sales increased 1% year over year. Those measures use different reporting bases, so investors shouldn’t confuse underlying adjusted growth with the change in reported revenue.
For the full year, 3M raised adjusted earnings guidance to $9.10 to $9.15 per share, incorporating a new reporting basis. That qualification matters because investors should compare the updated outlook with historical figures prepared on a consistent basis rather than assume the entire change reflects stronger operations.
Coherent stock’s 1.33% gain and Corning stock’s 0.21% decline provided a useful contrast with 3M stock’s 6% jump. The uneven performance suggests investors were responding particularly strongly to 3M’s combination of company-specific developments rather than buying every optics-related stock equally.
The Industrial Select Sector SPDR ETF (NYSEARCA:XLI) rose 0.75% to $167.93, offering a broader industrial-sector comparison for 3M stock. Meanwhile, the SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust (NYSEARCA:SPY) gained 0.61% to $771.15.
Against those benchmarks, 3M stock’s advance was substantially stronger than either the industrial group or the broader market. The comparison supports viewing the earnings report and Amazon agreement as important catalysts, although a single session doesn’t establish a lasting performance trend.
3M now has two developments for investors to follow: delivery against the raised earnings outlook and progress converting the Amazon relationship into sales. The company could build confidence if stronger profitability accompanies sustained demand for optical connectivity and other data center products.
However, 3M’s warrant structure ties much of the potential equity participation to future commercial activity rather than revenue already earned. Investors should watch for how purchases develop and whether the resulting growth justifies any eventual dilution.
The takeaway is that 3M stock has both an earnings catalyst and a longer-term growth opportunity supporting the rally. Further gains may depend on execution, so investors should consider keeping their position sizes modest rather than treating the Amazon relationship as guaranteed future revenue.

Investors often choose between specialized materials innovators and broad conglomerates when seeking stability. Are you better off with the focused networking growth of Corning (GLW -0.36%) or the massive scale of Honeywell International (HON +1.59%)?
Corning dominates the market for specialty glass and optical fiber, which are essential for modern communication. Honeywell operates as a multi-industry giant, selling everything from cockpit electronics to warehouse systems. Both companies are adapting to a landscape where efficiency and connectivity define the next generation of industrial expansion.
Corning manufactures highly engineered glass and ceramic products for various global industries. It partners with technology leaders such as Qualcomm (QCOM +1.26%), Amazon (AMZN +0.07%), and Nvidia (NVDA -0.29%) to provide high-density optical interconnects for data centers. Customer concentration like this adds a layer of risk to the business, as just two customers account for nearly 28% of optical sales.
In FY 2025, revenue reached nearly $15.6 billion, representing growth of approximately 19.1% compared to the prior year. This increase helped drive net income to roughly $1.6 billion, a significant jump from the $506 million reported in 2024. The expansion in net margin, which measures the percentage of revenue kept as profit, suggests the company is benefiting from higher demand for tech stocks related to networking.
As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the current ratio is approximately 1.6x, indicating the company has $1.60 in current assets for every $1.00 in current liabilities. The debt-to-equity ratio is roughly 0.9x, which measures total debt relative to shareholder equity. Free cash flow, which is cash from operations minus capital expenditures, was nearly $1.4 billion for the fiscal year.
Honeywell provides mission-critical automation solutions for industrial markets, refineries, and power grids. The company manages a vast portfolio and recently reached a commercial agreement with Bombardier (BDRBF +4.75%) for avionics and propulsion technologies. Its strategic focus remains on high-growth areas like aerospace and building automation while it divests less profitable units like its warehouse solutions business.
In FY 2025, revenue reached nearly $37.4 billion, reflecting growth of approximately 7.8% over the previous year. Despite the top-line growth, net income fell to roughly $4.7 billion from the nearly $5.7 billion recorded in FY 2024. This resulted in a net margin of approximately 12.6%, which was a decrease from the 16.4% margin seen in the prior twelve-month period.
As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio was roughly 2.2x, indicating the company uses a significant amount of borrowed money to fund its operations. The current ratio, which measures a firm's ability to pay short-term obligations, was approximately 1.3x. Free cash flow was strong at nearly $5.4 billion, providing capital for dividends and the integration of new acquisitions.
Corning faces risks from high customer concentration, particularly in its display and optical communications segments. It also deals with global supply chain volatility and the potential for manufacturing interruptions at its 78 worldwide sites. The company is sensitive to currency fluctuations in Asia and Europe while navigating the competitive pressures of the solar sector and intellectual property protection.
Honeywell is currently managing significant litigation risks, including federal securities fraud class actions and matters related to Flexjet. The company also faces operational and cybersecurity risks, evidenced by recent settlements regarding government contracts. Managing a complex global business involves the difficult task of integrating newly acquired entities while divesting units that may impact segment profit.
Honeywell International currently appears cheaper on a price-to-sales basis, while Corning carries a higher multiple that likely reflects its faster recent revenue growth.

Which stock would I buy in 2026?
I'd go with Corning. The transformation this company is going through makes it one of the more interesting industrial stocks to watch right now.
Most investors still think of Corning as a glassmaker, but that picture is changing fast. In Q2 2026, optical communications revenue grew more than 30% year over year as AI data centers continue to demand more connectivity infrastructure. Solar is now a growing business adding meaningful scale. And the company laid out an ambitious plan to grow from roughly $20 billion in annualized revenue today to $40 billion by 2030, a target backed by deepening partnerships with Nvidia and Amazon.
Honeywell Technologies, now a focused automation and building technology company after completing its aerospace spinoff in June 2026, is executing well. Organic sales grew, orders jumped, and the full-year outlook was raised in Q2 2026. For investors who want steady industrial exposure, it is a solid choice.
But Corning is in the middle of something bigger. For investors with a long time horizon, owning a business mid-transformation, before the new story is fully reflected in the stock price, is often where the best long-term returns come from. That's where I'm putting my money.

Corning (GLW) Is Wiring the AI Boom. Can Its Valuation Keep Up?
Corning (NYSE:GLW) delivered the kind of quarter most companies would frame and hang on the wall. Core earnings per share jumped 30% in the second quarter, and management guided to even more growth ahead. The stock's reward, according to CNBC, was a 12% drop after the report, which dragged other optical stocks down with it.
That reaction says more about expectations than about the business. Corning makes specialty glass and ceramics, from the tough cover glass on smartphones to the panels inside TVs. Its biggest unit today sells optical fiber, cable, and connectors. That's the plumbing that moves data between servers inside sprawling data centers, which has rapidly transformed the company's outlook as detailed in recent analysis on Corning's market positioning. So investors are now paying for an artificial intelligence growth story. Whether that price still makes sense depends less on last quarter's beat than on how much of Corning's upgraded long-term plan is already baked into the shares.
Corning Is Moving Beyond Fiber Cables. AI Networking Could Be the Next Big Opportunity
Corning has spent well over a century turning materials science into products other companies design around. That matters here. Once a hyperscaler (a giant cloud operator) builds its network around a fiber and connectivity system, switching suppliers mid-buildout is slow and risky.
The clearest proof arrived in the second quarter. Amazon signed a multiyear, multibillion-dollar agreement for Corning's fiber, cable, and connectivity in its US data centers. NVIDIA struck a long-term partnership to expand Corning's US optical connectivity manufacturing capacity tenfold and its US fiber production capacity by more than 50%. While customers don't commit like that to a commodity vendor, market commentary remains mixed on entry timing after the recent surge, even as Jim Cramer says to wait for Corning (GLW) to fall further before jumping in.
Optical Communications sales climbed 32% to $2.07 billion, while segment net income rose 77%. Enterprise Networks, the part of the unit serving data centers, grew sales 65%. Margins back up the pricing power. Core operating margin reached 20.9%, up 190 basis points (1.9 percentage points), and core gross margin improved to 39.6%. Adjusted free cash flow hit $1.42 billion, against $451 million a year earlier.
Management also upgraded its Springboard plan at its investor day this spring. It now targets an annualized sales run rate of $20 billion by the end of 2026, $30 billion by the end of 2028, and $40 billion by the end of 2030. For the third quarter, Corning guided to core EPS of $0.85 to $0.89, roughly 28% growth. Operational momentum like this highlights why major optical suppliers are catching broader interest, earning a mention alongside component peers featured in 12 High-Flying Stocks to Invest In.
What If AI Is the Only Engine?
The bear case is that Corning's growth is narrower than the headlines suggest. Glass Innovations, which now combines the old Display and Specialty Materials units, grew sales just 1%. Automotive rose 2%, and Life Sciences and Emerging Growth sales fell 15%. Solar sales jumped 90%, yet that segment still posted a small loss.
That ties the stock tightly to data center spending. If hyperscalers slow their buildouts, the business with the fastest growth is also the most exposed, a risk shared by other optical networking stocks like Coherent. The long-term Amazon and NVIDIA commitments soften that blow, but they don't remove it.
Here's where the debate gets sharp. Corning trades at 47.67 times forward earnings, as of October 9. That's well above the sector's 23.23 and its own five-year average of 24.26. Put simply, buyers are paying as if Corning were a very different company from the one that traded in the mid-20s for most of the past five years.
The growth outlook explains much of that premium. Expected EPS growth stands at 33.02% for 2027, and second-quarter core EPS growth of 30% shows the business is already running close to that pace. Yet, despite expanding its market footprint across fiber optics and specialized materials, the company doesn't make the cut among the 10 Best Aggressive Growth Stocks to Buy According to Wall Street Analysts. But a multiple this rich leaves little cushion. The post-earnings slide after a strong quarter shows how fast sentiment can sour when results are merely great. Corning asks you to pay up growth front that's still years away.
Hedge fund interest climbed, with 99 funds holding the stock in the most recent quarter, up from 91 in the prior one. Short interest sits at 2.31% of the float, pointing to relatively limited bearish positioning.
The evidence suggests Corning's moat is widening, as its biggest customers lock in capacity for years. The valuation is the harder sell. At 47.67 times forward earnings, the stock already prices in much of the Springboard plan's ambition.
The setup suits patient, long-term investors who believe AI data center spending has years left to run and who can stomach sharp swings. If you need a margin of safety, it's thin here. Two things would change the picture quickly: a cooling in Optical Communications growth, or a third-quarter result that falls short of guidance when Corning reports later this month.
While we acknowledge the risk and potential of GLW as an investment, our conviction lies in the belief that some AI stocks hold greater promise for delivering higher returns and doing so within a shorter time frame. Going by the price targets, the mean estimate of $185.75 indicates a potential upside of 26.1%.
The average comprises 16 short-term price targets ranging from a low of $129.00 to a high of $238.00, with a standard deviation of $28.72. While the lowest estimate indicates a decline of 12.4% from the current price level, the most optimistic estimate points to a 61.6% upside. More than the range, one should note the standard deviation here, as it helps understand the variability of the estimates. The smaller the standard deviation, the greater the agreement among analysts.
While the consensus price target is highly sought after by investors, the ability and unbiasedness of analysts in setting price targets have long been questionable. And investors making investment decisions solely based on this tool would arguably do themselves a disservice.
However, an impressive consensus price target is not the only factor that indicates a potential upside in GLW. This view is strengthened by the agreement among analysts that the company will report better earnings than what they estimated earlier. Though a positive trend in earnings estimate revisions doesn't give any idea as to how much the stock could surge, it has proven effective in predicting an upside.

Here's What You Should Know About Analysts' Price Targets
According to researchers at several universities across the globe, a price target is one of many pieces of information about a stock that misleads investors far more often than it guides. In fact, empirical research shows that price targets set by several analysts, irrespective of the extent of agreement, rarely indicate where the price of a stock could actually be heading.
While Wall Street analysts have deep knowledge of a company's fundamentals and the sensitivity of its business to economic and industry issues, many of them tend to set overly optimistic price targets. Are you wondering why?
They usually do that to drum up interest in shares of companies that their firms either have existing business relationships with or are looking to be associated with. In other words, business incentives of firms covering a stock often result in inflated price targets set by analysts.
However, a tight clustering of price targets, which is represented by a low standard deviation, indicates that analysts have a high degree of agreement about the direction and magnitude of a stock's price movement. While that doesn't necessarily mean the stock will hit the average price target, it could be a good starting point for further research aimed at identifying the potential fundamental driving forces.
That said, while investors should not entirely ignore price targets, making an investment decision solely based on them could lead to disappointing ROI. So, price targets should always be treated with a high degree of skepticism.
There has been increasing optimism among analysts lately about the company's earnings prospects, as indicated by strong agreement among them in revising EPS estimates higher. And that could be a legitimate reason to expect an upside in the stock. After all, empirical research shows a strong correlation between trends in earnings estimate revisions and near-term stock price movements.
For the current year, two estimates have moved higher over the last 30 days compared to no negative revision. As a result, the Zacks Consensus Estimate has increased 0.2%.
Moreover, GLW currently has a Zacks Rank #2 (Buy), which means it is in the top 20% of more than 4,000 stocks that we rank based on four factors related to earnings estimates. Given an impressive externally-audited track record, this is a more conclusive indication of the stock's potential upside in the near term. Can Meta’s Fiber Partner Corning Capitalize On Rising AI Fiber Prices?
Mon, October 19, 2026 at 11:52 AM CDT 3 min read
Prices for specialized optical fiber used inside AI data centers are forecast to average more than five times their 2025 levels this year.
That could be good news for Corning Incorporated (NYSE:GLW), a major manufacturer of fiber-optic cables and connectivity equipment. The company has a supply agreement worth up to $6 billion with Meta Platforms Inc. (NASDAQ:META).
Corning's Optical Communications business is already booming. Second-quarter sales jumped 32% to $2.07 billion, while segment net income surged 77% to $438 million.
But CEO Wendell Weeks says higher fiber prices aren't the main reason.
Why Higher Fiber Prices Aren't the Whole Story
TrendForce released new research Monday forecasting a global optical fiber shortage of 180 million fiber-kilometers this year, with shortages potentially lasting until 2028.
TrendForce puts industry capacity utilization at 92%, while inventories have fallen to just one month's supply. Expanding production typically takes 18 to 24 months.
As fiber supplies tighten, major customers are signing long-term agreements to secure future deliveries.
Corning's agreement with Meta runs through 2030 and covers fiber, cables and connectivity products. Meta will also serve as the main customer for an expansion of Corning's North Carolina cable factory, giving the manufacturer committed demand as it increases production.
During July's earnings call, Wolfe Research analyst George Notter questioned Weeks about rising prices and the company's growing reliance on long-term agreements.
"The price is higher, but that really isn't how we're driving that profitability improvement," Weeks said.
Instead, Weeks credited higher-value connectivity products that help customers build networks faster and more cheaply.
Weeks added that Corning could sell more of its newest products if it had the capacity to manufacture them.
Wall Street Remains Bullish Despite Selloff
Corning shares have lost roughly half their value since hitting a record high in June, despite booming demand for its optical products.

Corning (GLW) Is Wiring the AI Boom. Can Its Valuation Keep Up?
Corning (NYSE:GLW) delivered the kind of quarter most companies would frame and hang on the wall. Core earnings per share jumped 30% in the second quarter, and management guided to even more growth ahead. The stock's reward, according to CNBC, was a 12% drop after the report, which dragged other optical stocks down with it.
That reaction says more about expectations than about the business. Corning makes specialty glass and ceramics, from the tough cover glass on smartphones to the panels inside TVs. Its biggest unit today sells optical fiber, cable, and connectors. That's the plumbing that moves data between servers inside sprawling data centers, which has rapidly transformed the company's outlook as detailed in recent analysis on Corning's market positioning. So investors are now paying for an artificial intelligence growth story. Whether that price still makes sense depends less on last quarter's beat than on how much of Corning's upgraded long-term plan is already baked into the shares.
Corning Is Moving Beyond Fiber Cables. AI Networking Could Be the Next Big Opportunity
Corning has spent well over a century turning materials science into products other companies design around. That matters here. Once a hyperscaler (a giant cloud operator) builds its network around a fiber and connectivity system, switching suppliers mid-buildout is slow and risky.
The clearest proof arrived in the second quarter. Amazon signed a multiyear, multibillion-dollar agreement for Corning's fiber, cable, and connectivity in its US data centers. NVIDIA struck a long-term partnership to expand Corning's US optical connectivity manufacturing capacity tenfold and its US fiber production capacity by more than 50%. While customers don't commit like that to a commodity vendor, market commentary remains mixed on entry timing after the recent surge, even as Jim Cramer says to wait for Corning (GLW) to fall further before jumping in.
Optical Communications sales climbed 32% to $2.07 billion, while segment net income rose 77%. Enterprise Networks, the part of the unit serving data centers, grew sales 65%. Margins back up the pricing power. Core operating margin reached 20.9%, up 190 basis points (1.9 percentage points), and core gross margin improved to 39.6%. Adjusted free cash flow hit $1.42 billion, against $451 million a year earlier.
Management also upgraded its Springboard plan at its investor day this spring. It now targets an annualized sales run rate of $20 billion by the end of 2026, $30 billion by the end of 2028, and $40 billion by the end of 2030. For the third quarter, Corning guided to core EPS of $0.85 to $0.89, roughly 28% growth. Operational momentum like this highlights why major optical suppliers are catching broader interest, earning a mention alongside component peers featured in 12 High-Flying Stocks to Invest In.
What If AI Is the Only Engine?
The bear case is that Corning's growth is narrower than the headlines suggest. Glass Innovations, which now combines the old Display and Specialty Materials units, grew sales just 1%. Automotive rose 2%, and Life Sciences and Emerging Growth sales fell 15%. Solar sales jumped 90%, yet that segment still posted a small loss.
That ties the stock tightly to data center spending. If hyperscalers slow their buildouts, the business with the fastest growth is also the most exposed, a risk shared by other optical networking stocks like Coherent. The long-term Amazon and NVIDIA commitments soften that blow, but they don't remove it.
Here's where the debate gets sharp. Corning trades at 47.67 times forward earnings, as of October 9. That's well above the sector's 23.23 and its own five-year average of 24.26. Put simply, buyers are paying as if Corning were a very different company from the one that traded in the mid-20s for most of the past five years.
The growth outlook explains much of that premium. Expected EPS growth stands at 33.02% for 2027, and second-quarter core EPS growth of 30% shows the business is already running close to that pace. Yet, despite expanding its market footprint across fiber optics and specialized materials, the company doesn't make the cut among the 10 Best Aggressive Growth Stocks to Buy According to Wall Street Analysts. But a multiple this rich leaves little cushion. The post-earnings slide after a strong quarter shows how fast sentiment can sour when results are merely great. Corning asks you to pay up growth front that's still years away.
Hedge fund interest climbed, with 99 funds holding the stock in the most recent quarter, up from 91 in the prior one. Short interest sits at 2.31% of the float, pointing to relatively limited bearish positioning.
The evidence suggests Corning's moat is widening, as its biggest customers lock in capacity for years. The valuation is the harder sell. At 47.67 times forward earnings, the stock already prices in much of the Springboard plan's ambition.
The setup suits patient, long-term investors who believe AI data center spending has years left to run and who can stomach sharp swings. If you need a margin of safety, it's thin here. Two things would change the picture quickly: a cooling in Optical Communications growth, or a third-quarter result that falls short of guidance when Corning reports later this month.
While we acknowledge the risk and potential of GLW as an investment, our conviction lies in the belief that some AI stocks hold greater promise for delivering higher returns and doing so within a shorter time frame. That could be good news for Corning Incorporated (NYSE:GLW), a major manufacturer of fiber-optic cables and connectivity equipment. Second-quarter sales jumped 32% to $2.07 billion, while segment net income surged 77% to $438 million. But CEO Wendell Weeks says higher fiber prices aren’t the main reason. Why Higher Fiber Prices Aren’t the Whole Story TrendForce released new research Monday forecasting a global optical fiber shortage of 180 million fiber-kilometers this year, with shortages potentially lasting until 2028.TrendForce puts industry capacity utilization at 92%, while inventories have fallen to just one month’s supply. Expanding production typically takes 18 to 24 months. As fiber supplies tighten, major customers are signing long-term agreements to secure future deliveries. During July’s earnings call, Wolfe Research analyst George Notter questioned Weeks about rising prices and the company’s growing reliance on long-term agreements. “The price is higher, but that really isn’t how we’re driving that profitability improvement,” Weeks said. Instead, Weeks credited higher-value connectivity products that help customers build networks faster and more cheaply. Weeks added that Corning could sell more of its newest products if it had the capacity to manufacture them.
